title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: What is the key difference between a workflow and an agent?

options.text: A workflow never calls a language model, while an agent always calls one
In a workflow, code written ahead of time sets the steps; in an agent, the model chooses them
A workflow can only answer from training, while an agent is allowed to use tools
In a workflow, the model chooses the steps; in an agent, the programmer fixes their order

items.stem: Which of these makerspace assistant designs is an agent?

options.text: Code always runs check_calendar, then book_slot, then asks the model to write a confirmation
Code sorts each question by keyword, then sends it to either the manual search or the calendar
Code runs three prompts in a fixed order, and each model reply is pasted into the next prompt
The model is given three tools and picks which to call, in what order, and when to stop

items.stem: A makerspace program always runs three steps in this order: (1) the model pulls the machine name out of the question, (2) the code looks up that machine's manual page, (3) the model writes an answer from the page. Who owns the control flow, and what is this system?

options.text: The code owns it, so this is a workflow, even though the model does work in two steps
The model owns it, because it performs two of the three steps and so decides what happens
The code owns it, but the model is called twice, so this counts as an agent
The model owns it, because the model writes the final answer that the student reads

items.stem: A teammate says: "Booking a machine always goes check the calendar, then reserve the slot, then send a confirmation, so let's build it as an agent because agents are more advanced." Given a small model budget, what is the best reply?

options.text: Agree: an agent handles these same steps more reliably because it reasons about each one
Agree: an agent is cheaper here, because the model only calls the tools it turns out to need
Disagree: the steps are known and identical every time, so a fixed workflow does it with predictable cost and is easier to test
Disagree: a workflow cannot use a language model, so it could not write the confirmation message

items.stem: A student question needs the calendar, the manuals and the training record. As an agent, the model requests those three tools one at a time and then writes its final answer, and each model call ends with one tool request or the final answer. A fixed workflow handles the same kind of question with exactly 2 model calls every time. Across 50 such questions, how many more model calls does the agent make than the workflow, in total?

A program asks the model to draft a booking confirmation. Code then checks that the machine and date match the booking. If they do not, the code asks the model to draft again, up to 3 drafts in total, and then stops with an error. Is this a workflow or an agent?

options.text: An agent, because it loops until the result is right
A workflow, because the code sets the retry rule and the limit, and the model only writes text each time
An agent, because it makes more than one model call for a single request
A workflow only if it never retries; once it retries, the model is steering
